item.title: Bangladesh vows to arrest Hasina if she returns from India
item.description:
Bangladesh will arrest and jail former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina if she returns from India, a senior government minister said, as her plans to come home in December fuel political tension and renewed street violence.

Dhaka is instead seeking Hasina’s extradition from India, where she has lived since fleeing Bangladesh in 2024, and expects New Delhi to comply with an existing extradition treaty, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam told Reuters.

India’s foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In April, the ministry said it was examining Bangladesh’s request to extradite Hasina.

Hasina faces a death sentence in Bangladesh and her Awami League party is banned following the 2024 uprising that ended her long rule. The United Nations has said as many as 1,400 people were killed during the unrest.

Hasina fled Dhaka in August 2024 as protests demanding her resignation swept the country. She has since sought a new passport and identity card ahead of a planned return in December, requests the government has rejected.

“As soon as she tries to enter Bangladesh, she will be arrested. And she will be taken to jail, and the law will take its course,” Obaed said in an interview on Sunday.

“We would like India to honour the extradition treaty and return her as a convict, and the law will take its course. She (Hasina) will have to face the music.” The standoff has brought Hasina’s Awami League supporters out on the streets. The party this month announced a week of protests and rallies in support of Hasina’s return, culminating in a nationwide lockdown on November 19.

Police have recorded dozens of crude bomb blasts and incidents of arson targeting vehicles in at least 28 districts over the past 10 days, with several police officers and civilians injured, according to local media.

Obaed called the violence a survival tactic by Hasina’s “politically bankrupt political party.” Khalid Mahmud Chowdhury, a senior Awami League official, said the current political establishment was responsible for the violence.

The minister said there had been no official discussions with India about sending an aircraft to bring Hasina back, adding that Dhaka wanted balanced ties with New Delhi that did not compromise Bangladesh’s “dignity, self-respect and interests.” “India needs to decide what kind of foreign policy they need to adopt for Bangladesh,” Obaed said.

Rohingya verdict

Dhaka is also stepping up diplomatic pressure on neighbouring Myanmar over the return of Rohingya refugees after the UN’s highest court ruled that thousands of killings and widespread sexual violence by Myanmar’s security forces against the Muslim minority in 2017 amounted to state-sponsored genocide.

Myanmar has criticised the ruling by the International Court of Justice, saying Rohingya would only be able to return “when situations permit”.

“Now, this verdict gives us, Bangladesh, the strength, the Rohingya community the strength to fight,” Obaed said, adding that they deserved to return “with dignity and safety”.

About 1.2 million Rohingya live in Bangladesh after repeated repatriation attempts failed. Their return has been complicated by Myanmar’s civil war and the Arakan Army militia’s control of nearly all of Rakhine State, which is home for most Rohingya.

Obaed called for greater international pressure on Myanmar and the Arakan Army.

“Bangladesh did not create this crisis. Myanmar created this crisis, so Myanmar has to end it,” she said.

Security stepped up along border to prevent entry of ‘controversial’ persons
item.description:
Border security has been strengthened to prevent any controversial individuals from entering Bangladesh in December, said Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) Director General Major General Mohammad Ashrafuzzaman Siddiqui.

He made the remarks in response to a question from journalists after inspecting the Akhaura International Immigration Checkpost in Brahmanbaria on Sunday afternoon.

Earlier, he arrived by helicopter at the Hirapur School playground in Akhaura at around 3:30 pm.

BGB Director General Ashrafuzzaman Siddiqui said it was the responsibility of the BGB to guard the country’s entire border. Its duties included preventing smuggling and ensuring that no one could travel illegally across the border in either direction.

“As part of that responsibility, border security has been strengthened, particularly during this month of December, to prevent any illegal individuals or controversial figures from entering Bangladesh, while also preventing anyone from leaving the country illegally. We also want to prevent push-ins, drug smuggling, and the entry of weapons and explosives,” he said.

Ashrafuzzaman Siddiqui said, “That is why I am inspecting the border areas of Feni, Cumilla and Akhaura today. We have strengthened our security arrangements to ensure that these objectives are met. We must implement the government’s directives and fulfil the expectations of the country and its people. I have come here today to inspect the situation on the ground and ensure that border security is maintained to the fullest extent possible.”

Seeking cooperation from local residents, the BGB chief said, “Those of you who live in the area often have access to a great deal of information. If you learn of anyone planning to enter or leave the country, please inform us. If you share such information with the BGB, we will take appropriate measures to prevent it, Insha’Allah.”

BGB Regional Commander Brigadier General Saiful Islam, Sarail Sector Commander Colonel Rakib Hasan, 25 BGB Battalion Commander Lieutenant Colonel Jabbar Ahmed and other relevant officials were present during the visit.

item.title: COP31 fails to agree climate deal in chaotic finale
item.description:
TURKEY-AUSTRALIA-UN-CLIMATE-COP31

The COP31 climate talks headed for a historic defeat Sunday after the EU and other countries refused to endorse a pact that omitted fossil fuels as the summit lurched into record overtime in Turkey.

The main deal was rejected by a host of nations 44 hours after the summit’s official close in a chaotic COP31 finale in the Turkish city of Antalya.

“We will not endorse a cover decision... that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change,” said Ireland’s climate minister, Darragh O’Brien, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency.

COP31 President Murat Kurum conceded the deal had failed to reach consensus.

“I understand that there is no agreement on this text. For that reason, these decisions have not been adopted,” he told the closing session.

Fossil fuels are a flashpoint at the climate talks, which come against a difficult backdrop of soaring energy prices and geopolitical tensions stemming from the war between the United States and Iran that has roiled the Middle East.

Language around fossil fuels is fiercely opposed by petrostates such as Saudi Arabia.

With expectations low, negotiations chief Australia had sought an overarching “cover decision” to capture what countries agreed at COP31 and send a signal about the future course of climate action.

But the final proposal failed to mention coal, oil and gas at all, plunging the summit into turmoil as it broke the record for the longest-ever UN climate conference.

“We will not compromise our future to benefit fossil fuel interests. We will not accept an outcome that undermines our security and threatens our future,” the Marshall Islands climate envoy Kathy Jetnil-Kijiner told delegates.

Panama, a vocal critic of the UN climate talks, Vanuatu and Belize also rejected the pact.

Outside the assembly hall, O’Brien told AFP the summit had been “hijacked by some oil states”.

Decisions at the UN climate talks are taken by consensus, meaning just one of the nearly 200 nations involved can block agreement.

‘Licence to keep polluting’

Threats of a walkout Saturday prompted Turkey and Australia to convene a hurried meeting between the European Union and Saudi Arabia but a compromise remained elusive.

The latest text introduces an oblique reference to a previous global deal in 2023 to shift the world away from fossil fuels but stops short of naming them explicitly.

The text also proposed retaining a push to expand carbon capture, a technology championed by the fossil fuel industry but criticised as costly and ineffective in cutting emissions.

“We believe that climate change requires all solutions on the table and that countries select from these solutions depending on their national circumstances,” said Saudi climate negotiator Mohammad Ayoub, who spoke on behalf of the wider Arab Group of nations.

Climate campaigners had urged countries to reject the deal.

“This text isn’t a climate plan. It’s a licence to keep polluting,” said Sara Shaw of environmental group 350.org.

The summit had been under pressure to show progress on tackling soaring greenhouse gas emissions in a year of climate-linked disasters from Europe to Nepal and Indonesia.

Facing blowback over fossil fuels, Turkey and Australia pointed to “electrification” as a way to cut heat-trapping emissions and bolster energy security.

This works by replacing technologies that burn fossil fuels directly -- like diesel cars and gas heating -- with electric alternatives.

‘Profound disappointment’

The draft calls for global efforts to boost the share of electricity in total final energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035 and the expansion of “clean energy”.

But it does not explicitly require that electrification be powered by renewable energy. Around one-third of global electricity is produced using coal and another fifth using fossil gas.

Attempts by Saudi Arabia, India and Kenya meanwhile to delay the next major reports by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) have been another major source of friction at the talks.

The draft text “highlights the importance” of these reports for an upcoming stocktake of global carbon-cutting efforts in 2028.

Dozens of countries across Europe, Africa and the Pacific want these assessments by the IPCC, the global authority on climate science, published in time for that crucial stocktake.

Countries have also disagreed at COP31 over how to respond to the looming breach of the 1.5C warming target set under the Paris climate accord.

The latest draft expressed “deep concern” that global warming would cross 1.5C but some countries lamented the text did not go further.

“We are profoundly disappointed by the substance of the cover decision,” said UK climate negotiator Kate Hughes.

“It moves us backwards on the science... It is a lowest common denominator where it should have been, instead, presenting bold collective ambition on climate action.”

The talks also jammed over long-running complaints that rich nations are shirking their obligations to help developing nations confront climate change.

The removal of a $120-billion target for climate adaptation angered developing nations.

“We need finance, yet our partners showed up to this COP with empty hands,” said Jetnil-Kijiner of the Marshall Islands.

“We cannot do this on our own. We cannot survive on empty promises.”

item.title: Bhutan seeks Dhaka’s support for WHO candidature
item.description:
Former Bhutanese Prime Minister Sangay Ngedup on Sunday met State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir to discuss his candidature for the post of Regional Director of the World Health Organization's South-East Asia Regional Office (WHO SEARO).
During the meeting at the foreign ministry, Ngedup briefed the state minister on his candidature and outlined his vision for strengthening regional cooperation in the public health sector, according to a foreign ministry press release.
Ngedup, who previously served as Bhutan's Minister of Health and Education, is his country's candidate for the WHO SEARO regional director position.
During the meeting, he highlighted his priorities for enhancing public health cooperation among WHO member states in Southeast Asia.
WHO SEARO serves 11 member countries, including Bangladesh and Bhutan, coordinating regional efforts to strengthen health systems, address public health challenges and improve access to healthcare services.
The meeting came as Bhutan is promoting Ngedup's candidature for the regional leadership position.

item.title: Nahid calls for anti-fascist unity after returning from UK
item.description:
National Citizen Party (NCP) Convener and Opposition Chief Whip Nahid Islam has called for renewed anti-fascist unity upon returning from a week-long visit to London, accusing the BNP of undermining national unity by disregarding reform proposals and the July Charter referendum verdict.
Speaking to reporters at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport on Sunday evening, Nahid said the NCP had been the first to call for national unity on August 5. However, he alleged that the BNP had undermined that unity by disregarding the reform proposals and the verdict on the July Charter.
He also blamed the government's failure for the ongoing anarchy allegedly involving Awami League activists.
Nahid further claimed that he had been attacked in the United Kingdom with the intention of killing him. According to him, Awami League leaders and activists had planned the attack through an online meeting.
"Expatriate brothers and sisters stood as a shield and protected us," he said, adding that the matter had been brought to the attention of the government and local authorities.
Addressing the country's deteriorating law and order situation, Nahid said he had repeatedly raised concerns in parliament before leaving the country, warning about the worsening situation over the past seven months.
He said a report published six months after the government took office had identified law and order as the country's most critical area of concern.
He attributed the current situation to what he described as the government's indifference.

item.title: Minimum Wage Board meets Monday; RMG owners set to submit wage proposal
item.description:
The third meeting of the Minimum Wage Board will be held on Monday to review recommendations before determining a new wage structure for ready-made garment (RMG) workers, with factory owners expected to submit their new wage proposal at the session.
The meeting is scheduled for 11:30am at the Department of Labour in the capital, presided over by Board Chairman and Judge Syed Azad Subhani.
An earlier meeting slated for November 16 was postponed due to unavoidable circumstances, after which a notice announced the new date.
The board is expected to review opinions from worker and employer representatives along with relevant issues to move forward with drafting its minimum wage recommendations.
At its first meeting on November 4, the board instructed both sides to prepare and submit their respective wage structure proposals at the next sitting.
Subsequently, at the second meeting on November 9, worker representative Babul Akhter presented a four-grade monthly minimum wage structure for workers, proposing Tk48,000 for Grade 1, Tk43,000 for Grade 2, Tk38,000 for Grade 3, and Tk32,000 for Grade 4, alongside Tk30,000 for newly recruited or apprentice workers.
For office staff and employees, the workers' side proposed Tk55,000 in Grade 1, Tk50,000 in Grade 2, Tk45,000 in Grade 3, and Tk40,000 in Grade 4.
Employers were unable to submit their proposal at the second meeting; although they sought seven working days, the board granted four working days, setting a November 15 deadline for submission.
Currently, the minimum monthly wage for RMG workers stands at Tk12,500, which was announced in November 2023 and took effect in December that year, up from Tk8,000 set in 2018. Worker organizations have long been campaigning for a revised minimum wage—with broader demands pressing for at least Tk 30,000 a month—citing rising prices of essentials, house rent, healthcare, and overall living costs.
The government formed the six-member Minimum Wage Board on November 1, chaired by District and Sessions Judge Syed Azad Subhani, with Dhaka University Public Administration Professor Dr Mosleh Uddin Ahmed as the neutral member.
Representing employers are Bangladesh Employers’ Federation Joint Secretary General Asif Ayub and Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) Director ABM Shamsuddin, while workers are represented by Bangladesh Jatiyatabadi Sramik Dal President Anwar Hossain and Bangladesh Garments and Industrial Workers Federation General Secretary Babul Akhter.

item.description:
Bangladesh and Australia on Sunday discussed ways to deepen bilateral cooperation, particularly in trade, investment and energy security, alongside expanding partnerships in skills development, education and mobility.
The issues featured during a courtesy meeting between Australian High Commissioner to Bangladesh Susan Ryle and Foreign Secretary Salahuddin Noman Chowdhury at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs here.
During the meeting, the two diplomats exchanged views on a range of bilateral issues, focusing on opportunities to strengthen economic engagement and broaden cooperation in areas of mutual interest.
They also discussed cooperation in skills development, education and mobility, reflecting the growing importance of human resource development and people-to-people exchanges in bilateral relations.
The Rohingya crisis also featured in their discussions as Bangladesh continues to engage international partners on the longstanding humanitarian issue.

item.title: It’s Time to Settle With Russia
item.description: In October, U.S. President Donald Trump sold his eleventh-hour deal to secure diesel from Russian President Vladimir Putin—pausing sanctions that his own administration had imposed—as a boon for the negotiations to end the war in Ukraine. The arrangement, he wrote on Truth Social, was intended to keep Russia at “the bargaining table.” Of course, it was always obvious to observers that the gambit had as much or more to do with bolstering the U.S. economy and stemming a massive victory for the Democrats in this month’s midterm elections, and in that, it failed.Cynics have grounds for questioning all of Trump’s moves when it comes to Russia and Ukraine. He clearly dislikes Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and shows a marked preference for illiberal leaders, especially those willing to give him easy wins. Still, a stopped clock can be right twice a day. And concessions such as the fuel deal are exactly what might move Russia and Ukraine closer to peace, even if they are not wholly motivated by public-spiritedness.

item.title: The Time of the East Is Coming: Pakistans Ambassador on Trade, Trains, and Ties with Russia
North Korea Is Outsourcing Its Cybercrime Empire: Here’s How
item.description:
The software developer on the video call seemingly checks every box. He has a real face, a steady internet connection and a polished answer to every technical question. In reality though, he could be an Iranian or a South African developer who is being paid a few hundred dollars a month to play the part.

Once a U.S. company sends an offer letter and a work laptop, he steps aside. A North Korean operative, often working from China or Russia, logs in under the same name, does the job, sends the salary back to Pyongyang and quietly gains a foothold inside the company’s systems.

This is the newest twist in North Korea’s fake IT worker scheme. According to U.S. authorities, the state-run operation slips regime workers into remote tech jobs at Western companies under stolen or invented identities. The practice is growing as the regime’s hackers pull off the biggest thefts in cryptocurrency history, and the two efforts are more closely tied than most employers realize.

On Oct. 31, the FBI attributed the theft of more than $6 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance, the world’s largest exchange, to the North Korean hacking cluster known as TraderTraitor. The Oct. 29 heist, the largest on record, is roughly three times what North Korean-linked hackers stole in all of 2025. Binance has since said the breach started with a job interview, in which attackers posing as recruiters had one of its engineers download a coding “assignment” laced with malware onto his work computer.

If a single fake job interview could open the door to the largest crypto theft on record, what can a North Korean operative do once a company actually hires him?

The hiring side of Pyongyang’s cyber operation is moving just as fast. Material Security counted 2,429 suspected North Korean job seekers in the hiring pipelines it monitored over the past year, and reported that 27 of them made it to the onboarding phase of the hiring process. At one company where a persona was onboarded just last month, roughly 277,000 files containing Social Security numbers were made available company-wide or through public links. CrowdStrike, a cybersecurity firm that tracks state-backed hacking groups, says it uncovers one or two suspected North Korean IT worker cases every day.

Increasingly, the scheme runs on hired help from third countries. Recruits in Iran, Syria, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia and South Africa have been paid to pose as job applicants on camera, according to American officials and private researchers.

The stakes reach well beyond payroll fraud.

A United Nations panel of experts reported in 2024 that malicious cyber activity generates about half of North Korea’s foreign currency income and according to one member state, funds some 40 percent of its weapons of mass destruction programs. CrowdStrike has linked the IT worker campaign to North Korea’s Munitions Industry Department, which runs its weapons production. Once inside a company, those workers can reach source code, customer data and internal networks.

“The money matters because it funds the weapons program, but I think the access is the bigger concern,” Jason Vest, chief technology officer of Binary Defense, tells The Cipher Brief. “These are bad actors sitting inside U.S. networks with legitimate credentials, and North Korea can decide at any point that stealing data or crypto is worth more than the paycheck.”

So how does it all really work behind the scenes, and what is Pyongyang trying to achieve?

A $500-a-Month Face for the Camera

Experts believe the scheme draws on a workforce that North Korea has spent decades building. South Korea’s spy agency estimated in 2024 that the North’s cyber operations employ about 8,400 people. According to a recent Reuters investigation, children as young as 11-years-old are selected for computer science training. The best go to military cyber units and those who don’t make the cut are trained to build software for Western firms through remote work.

Those operatives, mostly based in China, Russia and Southeast Asia, build fake Western personas with polished LinkedIn profiles and GitHub histories. They apply for remote jobs by the thousands. Then they send someone else to the interview.

Internal documents obtained by the threat intelligence firm Flare show how the recruiting works. One North Korean facilitator, known as “Sea,” wrote “Targeting Iran guys” in a spreadsheet tracking recruits. Another, “Eugene,” noted he was “Hiring new guys in Iran, Syria and SA.” Flare identified at least 14 Iranians in the pipeline since 2024, and at least two reportedly received offer letters from American employers.

Recruits were offered about $500 a month in cryptocurrency to work part-time as “interview associates,” with pay climbing to as much as $5,000 a month once a job was secured. Each stand-in was assigned a made-up American persona, such as “Jack Long,” a fake C#/.NET developer. When a stand-in failed an interview, the facilitator reviewed the recording and coached him for the next one.

The goal is straightforward. Every stand-in who clears an interview opens a job for a North Korean operator, and every job brings a paycheck for the regime and a login that gains access inside an American company. Flare’s documents show facilitators chasing blockchain jobs, onboarding at an American credit union and closing in on a position at one of the largest defense contractors in the United States.

The stand-ins are found the way any freelancer is. Kudelski Security, a Swiss firm, described developers in Iran, Syria and South Africa as ordinary citizens who accepted offers on LinkedIn. Flare researchers found that one recruiter’s pitch asked outright whether candidates were comfortable working under someone else’s identity, while dangling crypto payments that sidestep Iran’s banking embargo. Recruits knew they were lending their faces to someone else’s résumé, though the documents don’t show that all of them knew the someone else was North Korea.

For Pyongyang, who sits in front of the camera matters far less than what happens after the call. Justin Hastings, a professor of international relations and comparative politics at the University of Sydney, says North Korean sanctions evasion has long relied on third-country partners acting as the regime’s interface with the outside world.

“The North Koreans themselves aren’t in peril, and the third-party cut-outs are disposable from their perspective. The North Koreans want the money, and the access — who actually meets with the company is less important to them,” Hastings tells The Cipher Brief.

In other words, when a stand-in is caught, the Iranian or South African faces the consequences. The North Korean behind him recruits another face.

Why Sanctions Keep Missing the Mark

The move to foreign stand-ins is partly a result of Western success. Companies learned to catch North Koreans using AI face filters when they asked candidates to wave a hand in front of the camera or to insult North Korean leader Kim Jong Un on the spot. It seems a real person from Tehran or Johannesburg passes those tests easily.

“Just about every criminal scheme in history has adapted to bypass controls intended to stop it,” Alex Hamerstone, advisory solutions director at TrustedSec, tells The Cipher Brief.

Vest describes it as an evolution of the threat.

“Companies have gotten better at spotting deepfakes and camera tricks during video interviews, so North Korea started paying real people to take the interview for them,” he says. “Once the stand-in gets the job, a North Korean operator does the actual work.”

Washington has thrown indictments, raids and sanctions at the problem, with limited effect. On Oct. 14, the Justice Department announced charges against 14 people after FBI agents raided more than 40 suspected “laptop farms” in Texas, homes where facilitators keep company-issued computers so operatives overseas can appear to be working from the United States.

Prosecutors say the devices helped put North Korean workers inside more than 70 American companies. The Treasury Department has sanctioned facilitators from Vietnam to Spain, and a later round on Oct. 28 hit Russians accused of cashing out crypto for the network.

Each designation, however, catches a front company or an intermediary, and new ones replace them. Treasury estimates the IT worker program brought in nearly $800 million in 2024. The security firm DTEX traced about $1.97 million in worker payments through Korea Ryonbong General Corporation, a sanctioned defense company, and found that money moving through the network helps fund Russia’s war in Ukraine.

Hamerstone underscores that North Korea is already so isolated that additional sanctions are unlikely to have much effect, and prosecutions run into a numbers problem.

“If the quantity of individuals available to perpetrate a crime far exceeds the number who are caught and punished, the indictments are unlikely to have a significant effect on the proliferation of the activity,” he explains.

Vest sees the same gap from the defender’s side.

“Sanctions don’t do much against a country that’s already cut off, and the people getting indicted are never going to see a U.S. courtroom,” he explains. “The place this can be stopped is the hiring process at American companies, and right now it’s still too easy to get through.”

From Paycheck to Heist

It isn’t only corporate payrolls. On July 28, Todd Hemmen, a deputy assistant director in the FBI’s Cyber Capabilities Branch, told a Washington conference that agents had identified a North Korean remote IT worker on a federal job the week before. He did not say which agency. People who follow federal hiring suspect a contractor, since direct government jobs come with background checks. Contract IT support work rarely gets that level of vetting, and it can still come with a login to government networks.

Defense work is a prime target. In one case, a worker using a stolen American identity spent more than two months inside a California defense contractor’s systems, downloading export-controlled technical data. When workers get inside particularly valuable targets, CrowdStrike says it has seen that access handed to North Korean malware teams to collect intelligence. And when workers are exposed and fired, the FBI warns, some hold stolen source code and data for ransom.

Crypto companies sit at the center of the overlap. Chainalysis has found that North Korea pulls off its outsized heists by embedding IT workers inside crypto services to gain privileged access. In April, the trading platform Drift Protocol lost about $285 million in an operation it tied to a North Korean state-affiliated group, and said the people who met its team face to face were not North Korean nationals. Binance shows the reverse side of the same hiring channel, with North Korean hackers posing as the recruiters.

Hastings notes that the regime’s motives line up with its other revenue operations.

“As with everything related to North Korea’s money-making schemes, they want to make money, and the opportunity for espionage and information gathering is a bonus,” he stresses.

Hamerstone argues the distinction matters less than it seems.

“I don’t believe it is one or the other,” he observes. “Reports show that a significant portion of North Korea’s money comes from these types of activities, and if the assumption that North Korea having resources is a problem, then anything that provides additional funding to them is an issue.”

What Hiring Managers Keep Missing

Flare concluded “with high confidence” that North Korean operatives are deliberately targeting American defense contractors, cryptocurrency exchanges and financial institutions, where a single insider can do the most damage. In 2024, the security firm KnowBe4 says it caught a newly hired North Korean worker loading malware onto his company-issued Mac within minutes of receiving it.

The red flags tend to show up after the offer letter goes out. A new hire’s video stops working, or he asks for the company laptop to be shipped to an address that doesn’t match his résumé, or his payroll account changes a few weeks into the job. Network logs often trace his logins to a commercial VPN, and one company came up so often that the fraud-detection firm Spur published a free list of the service’s IP addresses so employers could screen for it.

At many companies, though, no single person is watching for any of this. HR runs the hiring and security runs the network, so the two sets of warning signs rarely end up in the same place.

Hamerstone points out that no single missing control is to blame.

“Employee vetting is not as strong and thorough as it should be, especially for remote roles with access to organizational resources,” he notes. “This ends up becoming even more of an issue because many organizations have weak access control within the organization, limited monitoring of employee access, and other missing foundational security controls.”

The FBI’s advice is old-fashioned: verify identity in person where possible and hold part of onboarding face to face. Third-country stand-ins make that harder. The person who shows up to an in-person meeting may be real and still may not be the person doing the work.

For Vest, the problem starts with how companies think about identity.

“They verify identity once, during the interview, and assume the person who shows up to work is the same one,” he adds. “Check again at onboarding, only ship laptops to verified addresses, and pay attention when a new hire is running remote access tools or logging in from somewhere that doesn’t match.”

item.description: On November 1, news broke that hackers from the Belarusian Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow had breached the website of Rosstat, Russia’s federal statistics agency, and obtained data on Russian military losses in the war through fall 2026. The hackers used that data to produce their own estimate of how many Russians had been killed on the front lines. They also shared the database with reporters, including those at Meduza and Mediazona, which have been tracking Russia’s military death toll together for several years. We examined the hacked database and concluded that it was very likely authentic. We then compared its records with other sources and ran a new analysis. Our earlier studies relied mainly on data from the Register of Inheritance Cases. The Rosstat database makes the new estimate more reliable. Another important change: The new estimate counts both registered deaths and missing service members, many of whom will likely be confirmed dead.

item.title: Europe should fund Ukraine’s defence industry as a partner, not a supplier
item.description:
Europe should fund Ukraine’s defence industry as a partner, not a supplier Expert comment jon.wallace 23 November 2026

Ukraine’s strikes on the Kerch Bridge and Russian navy show the extent of its defence industry’s abilities. The EU 2027 finance package should seek to boost that industry towards a lasting partnership.

In mid-November, Ukrainian forces destroyed a road span of the Kerch Bridge, linking occupied Crimea to mainland Russia. The strike used jet-powered drones and cruise missiles reportedly guided through an airborne relay network rather than Starlink. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the bridge strike as the seventh phase of an operation that had first targeted the air-defence, radar and electronic warfare systems protecting the crossing. 

Sequencing of that kind, combining several weapon types using communications under Ukrainian control, owes much to Ukrainian military planning. But the weapons and the relay network themselves reflect a Ukrainian defence sector that has learned to design, field and adapt systems in months, rather than the years typical of European procurement. 
The strike package was not wholly Ukrainian: Destinus, a Dutch-headquartered company, says its systems were the only foreign-made weapons used. Russia’s embassy in The Hague responded by asking publicly whether the Netherlands had joined the war. 

Days later, on 22 November, Kyiv said seven Ukrainian-made sea drones had successfully sunk the Russian corvette Merkury at the Benghazi Naval base in Libya. Unlike Kerch, this attack appears to have involved no foreign weapons, showing the kind of low-cost maritime capability Ukraine has developed and can exercise at range.

Ukraine’s innovation advantage

Ukraine’s defence industry has developed under conditions that no European procurement system faces. Weapons and systems are tested in an active warzone, providing immediate operational feedback and demanding compressed procurement cycles. Its production capacity has grown from around $1 billion in 2022 to an estimated $35 billion in 2025. EU member states together spent €418 billion on defence that year, so Ukraine’s edge is the speed of its innovation.

The tempting conclusion is that a country able to produce such technology under these pressures can build anything Europe needs, including air defence, if the money is there. Indeed, Kyiv has called on partners to help build ‘the arsenal of the free world’ with Ukraine. However, operational effectiveness should not be confused with industrial capacity. 

Know-how is not the main constraint: Ukraine inherited much of the Soviet Union’s missile-design base, and its companies are now developing ballistic and anti-ballistic missiles alongside unmanned systems. 

The binding constraints are instead access to capital, production capacity, industrial facilities that are vulnerable to Russian attacks, and the availability of specialist components, particularly advanced electronics and seekers.

Of these, finance is the most immediate concern. The head of Ukraine’s Council of Defence Industry has said that manufacturers are operating at around 40 per cent of their potential capacity because the government is not placing enough orders. That suggests that additional funding could quickly unlock production potential. 

However, Europe’s requirements go beyond volume. Advanced air defence, particularly against ballistic missiles, depends on complex radar and sensor networks, high-end interceptors and industrial supply chains that require substantial investment and sustained development. Ukraine’s experience can inform European capability development. But it does not remove the need for Europe to build and maintain such capabilities itself.

The limits of a supplier relationship

There are other limitations on purchasing from Ukraine. Kyiv’s export framework is designed to protect its own forces. Companies may export only if they can also fulfil Ukrainian government contracts. Exports carry no intellectual property rights. And re-export requires Kyiv’s approval and attracts a 20 per cent tax.  

Even the drones built at the first Ukrainian joint venture in Germany are currently allocated to Ukraine’s armed forces. These are rational choices for a country fighting for its survival. But they mean that in a crisis, European governments could not assume Ukrainian output would be available for their own requirements, at least until Kyiv’s rules adapted.

A ceasefire would raise a different problem extending beyond supply-chain security. Ukraine’s advantage is tied to the operational environment in which its firms develop and test equipment. A settlement would necessarily reduce the operational feedback, procurement incentives and pressure that drive innovation. European planning should not assume that the wartime model will persist, or that Ukraine’s production priorities will stay aligned with Europe’s.

Closer cooperation also carries political risk: Moscow’s reaction to Destinus fits a pattern of embassy statements labelling Dutch support for Ukraine as participation in the conflict. European governments should anticipate diplomatic coercion and hostile activity directed against facilities, personnel and supply chains associated with Ukrainian defence production. Russia has already named European firms producing drones for Ukraine as potential targets. In August, an explosive-laden drone was found beside a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at Leipzig/Halle airport, an attack Germany has since attributed to Russia. Such hybrid attacks could make some European governments more cautious about hosting joint production, underlining the importance of protecting facilities, personnel and supply chains.

From procurement to partnership

The European Commission’s proposed €45 billion loan to Ukraine for 2027, the second half of the EU’s €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan, including €31.7 billion for defence, provides an opportunity to shape cooperation. The allocation of these funds will have long-term consequences beyond Ukraine’s immediate military requirements. 

Funding can support Ukrainian production for domestic use, establish joint ventures on European territory, or, where EU rules allow a derogation, finance procurement from established suppliers outside Europe, including the United States. 

Buying Ukrainian output sustains Ukraine’s defence. And buying from outside Europe fills immediate gaps. But only joint ventures build enduring capacity across Europe. Ukraine’s immediate needs, particularly for air defence this winter, must remain central to European assistance. But joint ventures are where support and European industrial development can converge, and where a meaningful share of the package should be directed.

The partnership should rest on a division of labour that draws on what Ukraine’s circumstances have produced. The war has given Ukraine’s defence industry what European nations cannot match during peacetime: urgency, a tolerance for failure, and feedback loops that are measured in days. 

Reinforced by Kyiv stripping out procurement, testing and regulatory barriers, Ukraine’s industry benefits from low-cost mass production and rapid iteration under pressure. That has delivered interceptor drones and long-range strike at a pace and cost that European procurement has, to date, struggled to match. 

Partnership offers the rest of Europe a way to learn from Ukraine’s experience of rapid development and operational feedback, while reinforcing the need to reform Europe’s procurement systems. Ukraine is already offering foreign firms the chance to test equipment in near-combat conditions alongside frontline units, through its state-backed Brave1 defence-tech cluster, and to pair with Ukrainian manufacturers for co-production. European states should take up that offer as partners rather than customers. 

European states and companies, in turn, bring radar and sensor technology, high-end interceptors, sovereign space-based communications, capital, and production sites beyond the reach of Russian missiles. 

Joint ventures and licensed production can bring these together, but only if they involve genuine technology transfer, shared research, integrated supply chains, and appropriate allocation priority when the future security picture shifts. Ukrainian reporting has described the German joint venture as closer to a showcase than the start of a systematic process, whereas Destinus reports output approaching 300 Ruta missiles a month.

Moving from individual projects to an enduring framework will require predictable multi-year financing and agreements on intellectual property that give Ukrainian and European manufacturers the confidence to invest together.

European leaders should therefore ask not only how much to spend on Ukraine, but how that spending can future-proof collective European security and capability. Treating Ukraine as a source of weapons risks creating a dependency that becomes visible only when European security is next under pressure. Building shared industrial capacity would strengthen Ukraine’s defence and Europe’s resilience at the same time.

Atrocities happen again and again. We need a comprehensive framework that would allow us to predict, prevent or respond to them

For the first time a state, Myanmar, has been found directly responsible for the crime of genocide. item.title: Rohail Nazir's fifty books Asia Cup Rising Stars semi-finals spot for Pakistan Shaheens
item.description:
An unbeaten half-century by Rohail Nazir, followed by a devastating bowling display, helped Pakistan Shaheens defeat Nepal by 96 runs in their final Group ‘B’ match of the Asia Cup Rising Stars at the University of Doha for Science and Technology on Tuesday.

The defending champions remained unbeaten in the tournament, winning all three of their group matches to qualify for the semi-finals, where they will face Bangladesh A on Nov 27.

Batting first, Pakistan Shaheens were in trouble at 66-6 in 16.5 overs before wicket-keeper-batter Rohail steadied the innings with an unbeaten 64 off 83 balls, hitting four fours and three sixes.

After Hasan Nawaz fell for 28 off 59 balls, leaving the Shaheens at 88-7, Rohail added 70 runs for the eighth wicket with Ahmed Daniyal, who scored 16 off 35 balls, to help his side reach 168 before being bowled out in 42 overs.

For Nepal, Rashid Khan claimed five wickets for 39 runs, while Abhishesh Gautam took two.

Nepal’s chase got off to a disastrous start as Muhammad Imran and Mohammad Hasnain reduced them to 15-4 inside six overs. Hasnain struck twice in successive deliveries to dismiss Ishan Pandey and Lokesh Bam without scoring.

Left-arm spinner Sufyan Moqim then claimed three wickets as Nepal slumped to 59-9. Mayan Yadav offered some resistance with a top score of 41 off 50 balls but was trapped leg-before by Maaz Sadaqat as Nepal were dismissed for 72 in 17.3 overs.

Hasnain and Sufyan took three wickets each for 21 and 17 runs respectively, while Imran claimed two for 29.

Rohail was named player of the match for his match-winning innings.

item.title: Liberté, égalité, fatigué—the young are tired of everyone
item.description:
The writing was on the wall. Calls for mobilisation on 17 October had been followed by viral videos, parodying Japanese anime and Marvel productions to rally the troops. The streets had caught on: with each new day of mobilisation, walls became covered in angry, audacious graffiti, ranging from ‘F@ck the 17 (the generic number for the French police), bring on the 17th’ to ‘17 October, better than October 17 (the second of two revolutions in Russia in 1917)’.

When the day finally arrived, a perfect storm swept across France, from its largest metropolitan areas to its mid-sized towns. High school and university students, who had been mobilising for weeks, took to the streets in large numbers. They were joined by demonstrators protesting the rising cost of living, including some associating themselves with the Yellow Vest movement, as well as by French and foreign far-left activists. All in all, between 550,000 and 800,000 persons went into the streets on that day. In the violence that ensued, some turned on police forces and official buildings, while others targeted small businesses and department stores. Mass looting and damage to public buildings, including the town halls of Limoges and Marseille, led the government to impose curfews in several cities over the next few days.

In each city, even in each neighbourhood, this day of mobilisation took on a different character, depending on the composition of the crowds and their interactions with the police. In some parts of Paris, Marseille, Lyon, Nantes, Rennes or Bordeaux, the attacks against police forces and government buildings took a quasi-insurrectional character. Elsewhere, the riots were more reminiscent of the ordered disorder of carnival. As law enforcement remained at a distance, the streets were left to jubilant protesters, often dressed up in costumes. In this space wrested from the ordinary constraints of everyday life, the Republican motto of ‘liberté, égalité, fraternité’ (liberty, equality, fraternity) suddenly took a new meaning as protesters of different ages, classes and racial backgrounds revelled in the furious spectacle of their momentary unity. This subversion of the protest order — it was no longer the demonstration that overflowed, but the overflow that demonstrated — nevertheless remained contained within certain bounds. In the parts of Paris that I walked through, at least, vehicles and shops were not set on fire and the forces of disorder remained somewhat contained, at least until the looting began.

This day of wrath and jubilation will probably not be repeated soon. The stars that aligned on that day have since then changed their orbit. Suburban youths, many of them first-time protesters, have not been durably integrated into street protests, while the intensity of repression deterred more privileged youths from repeating the experience of the 17th. In the following weeks, the mobilisation thus took a less belligerent turn and returned to a more conventional social movement led by student and labour unions. In many lycées, however, blockades persist and tensions are rising between mobilised students and parents worrying about the impact of a prolonged closure of the schools.

A clap of thunder in a troubled sky

Calls for a mobilisation against ‘la vie chère’ (high cost of living) started circulating on social media in September 2026, autonomously from the labour unions that traditionally organise demonstrations in France. In September 2025, a similar attempt to ‘block everything’ across the country was a failure and French intelligence agencies did not take the hype around 17 October seriously. They miscalculated the amplifying effect of the student movement, without which this call to action would probably have fizzled out.

In September 2026, a nationwide movement of high school and university students started calling for better teaching conditions, including increased teaching staff and renovated school buildings. The mobilisation was also fuelled by a deep crisis within the French higher education system. In 1980, only 40 per cent of a whole age group obtained the baccalaureate. Today, 80 per cent obtain this prestigious school-leaving certificate, leading to severe pressure on higher education institutions. Rather than the increase of baccalaureate-holders per se, stagnant state funding of universities and limited vocational education options have severely constrained the access to higher education. While asking for 200,000 new positions in universities, high school students have also been asking for the suppression of Parcoursup, the pre-enrolment platform for first-year higher education programmes, which they see as opaque, discriminatory and stressful.

By protesting underfunding of high schools and universities, mobilised students also defended an idea of public education as a public good. As Leila, a 12th grade student in the 9th arrondissement of Paris, told me while sitting on a dustbin during the blockade of her high school on 5 November, “We are calling for pay rises for our supervisors, our cleaners and our teachers. We cannot expect teachers to work themselves to the bone if their salaries do not reflect the effort they put in. Our teachers are the backbone of education and teaching. And education is a weapon against disinformation and the dumbing down of society.”

The movement initially started in late August in Mayotte, an overseas department and region located in the Indian Ocean, before expanding to impoverished suburbs of the Greater Paris region, such as Créteil and Saint-Denis. With a significant number of them of North African or Sub-Saharan African descent, local students denounced the unkept promises of the French meritocratic system of education. By draping themselves in the national flag or singing the national anthem in protests, they reiterated their attachment to egalitarian ideals, while pointing out the systemic discrimination undermining the professed ideal of equal opportunity for descendants of postcolonial immigrants. By early October, the protests expanded to more privileged sections of the youths, including the so-called ‘jeunesse dorée’ (golden youth) attending the most prestigious public schools. Expressing solidarity with suburban youths, students from city centres shared their concern with the clogging of higher education, their anxieties towards the possibilities of the far-right Rassemblement National coming to power in 2027, as well as more diffuse fears towards a future compromised by the compounding threats of climate change, armed conflict and artificial intelligence.

Even if it does not yet translate into joint structures of mobilisation transcending deep social, racial and residential divides, the sense of unity among this anxious youth is palpable. Besides shared concerns specific to this age group, it is rooted in demographic transformations. In 2026, the number of people aged 65 and over became nearly equal to the number of those under 20, and this trend toward a demographic reversal will only intensify in the next decades. By 2070, 32 per cent of the population will be 65 or older — twice the proportion of those under 20. In this ageing society, which it holds responsible for the current state of world affairs, the youth feel belittled and silenced.

The brutal repression of the movement only added fuel to the fire. During the first weeks of October, protests spread to numerous high schools and universities, many of which were subsequently blockaded across the country. In the meantime, increasing price of petrol at the pumps and rising costs of living more generally stoked concerns about purchasing power. This led young influencers and activists to call for a resumption of the Yellow Vest movement, which was prompted by similar concerns in 2018. As 17 October approached, clashes with the police multiplied around high schools and during street demonstrations. In many cities, the atmosphere was electric.

Joyful anger

In its early phase and even more so on 17 October, this social movement disrupted the rules of political contention in France. Like the Yellow Vests before them, students initially evaded the control of labour unions that, historically, have been leading protests, articulating claims and negotiating with governmental authorities. Instead, high school and university students were mobilised by content on social media and they organised horizontally, through messaging applications like Snapchat. Their privileged forms of action were blockades and, to a lesser extent, wildcat demonstrations. Every morning, students would collect dustbins and building materials to block the entrance of their school, sometimes before going on an unauthorised demonstration across the area. On 1 October, I attended one such event in Saint-Denis, in the northern periphery of Paris. After assembling near Lycée Paul Éluard, about 200 high school and university students walked — and occasionally ran — across the town, visiting one high school after the other to mobilise other students. The mood was joyful but resolute: while provoking the police chasing them, students laughed, sang and delivered fiery speeches. Among the protesting students was a young boy dressed as Spider-Man and wearing a motorcycle helmet. Sitting on a dustbin pushed by jubilant teenagers, he was the focus of attention and added a dash of colour among young men and women often dressed in black and wearing surgical masks to protect themselves against tear gas.

As the movement expanded, student and labour unions started joining the fray and organising massive demonstrations across the country. These protests were more conventional in nature, and easier to manage for law enforcement. The large participation of high school and university students, however, endowed them with an energy and a creativity evading the usual mobilisations of labour unions. Expanding on a protest repertoire that emerged during the movement against the reform of pension laws in 2023, young participants brought placards with ironic, witty slogans drawing from various sources of influence: the Revolution of 1789, the protest movement of May 1968, as well as social media and popular culture. The reclaiming of revolutionary symbols — the caps of the sans-culottes, the guillotine, Liberty leading the people — coexisted with references to video games such as Mario Bros, Legend of Zelda or GTA, to popular film series such as Star Wars and the Hunger Games, as well as to more contemporary Internet memes and ‘brain rot’. Some of the slogans were franchised: after circulating on social media, they were picked up by young protesters, who in the process reaffirmed their belonging to a protest community united by shared cultural references.

As Céline, a student at EPSA, the Paris school of graphic design and visual communication, explained during a demonstration on 5 November, “popular culture allows you to convey political messages more easily, because everyone has the reference”. On that day, she was herself dressed up as Luigi, the secondary protagonist of the video game franchise Mario Bros, and she carried a placard showing this popular character removing President Emmanuel Macron and the far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen with a vacuum cleaner.

Indeed, beyond making claims for better working conditions in lycées and universities, these youthful protests have also been directed against the far right and the imminent threat of its access to power after the presidential elections of May 2027. Besides a general sense of dread towards an uncertain future, this threat has been a major unifier among the youth, across social and racial divides. Drawn from a song by the 1980s punk band Bérurier Noir, ‘La jeunesse emmerde le Front National’ (The youth tells the Front National [the original name of the Rassemblement National] to f@ck off) remains one of the popular anthems among the protesters, although a new one emerged in early November, ‘J’ai deux passions, la fanfare, la révolution’ (I have two passions: the brass band and the revolution!).

‘Everyone hates the police’, but the police have many friends

Both joyful and belligerent, this social movement has met with unprecedented levels of repression, which has fuelled hostility, even hatred towards the police. As of 17 November, at least 155 protesters or passers-by had suffered serious injuries by the explosive weapons used by law enforcement — including 11 eye losses, seven amputations and 18 fractured skulls. The number of arrests has also reached unprecedented levels: between mid-September and mid-November 2026, more than 12,000 protesters were sent to custody, most of them minors. By comparison, 6,730 protesters met the same fate during the 2018–2019 movement of the Yellow Vests, 890 during the protests against the reform of labour laws in 2016, 150 during the student movement against the Loi Devaquet in 1986 and only 95 during the uprising of May 1968.

Far from restraining law enforcement officers, the Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez has encouraged them to show “no restraint” when dealing with the protesters, whatever their age. Meanwhile, the Minister for Justice, Gérald Darmanin, has asked judges to be “merciless” with looters and rioters, especially after the events of 17 October. By and large, the judges have obliged and the judicial repression of the movement has been extremely severe, with large numbers of protesters being sent to jail for petty offences. During the days that followed 17 October, drastic measures were also taken to contain the protests.

Incidents of police violence have been widely publicised among the youths, through social media in particular. This has fuelled detestation of the police, exemplified by popular slogans heard at every demonstration: ‘ACAB’ (All Cops Are Bastards) or ‘Tout le monde déteste la police’ (Everyone hates the police).

Everyone does not hate the police in France, though. As a recent opinion poll by the Centre for Political Research at Sciences Po (CEVIPOF) shows, the level of confidence in the police remains high, at 73 per cent. Moreover, as violence escalated during protests and blockades dragged on, a growing number of individuals started volunteering to lend a strong hand to the police. Following the mass lootings that took place on 17 and 18 October, some influencers launched platforms to gather volunteers in support of shopkeepers. While the individuals behind these initiatives claimed to be politically neutral and to act in accordance with the law, the reality on the ground was rather different. On 24 October, as new protests were organised across the country, far-right militants assaulted demonstrators in a dozen cities under the pretext of protecting shopkeepers. Not only did the police refrain from interfering, in several cities, they actively collaborated with far-right groups, who delivered protesters to the men in blue after roughing them up. In Montpellier, a couple of days later, a judge sentenced one of these protesters to a suspended prison term after acknowledging that he had been arrested “by a militia“. After these collusions were exposed, several investigations were launched and far-right extremists became less visible in the following weeks, but the threat lingers on.

As high school blockades dragged on in many large cities, some parents also started acting as auxiliaries of law enforcement, if not as vigilantes taking the law in their own hands. Especially after the government of Sébastien Lecornu granted a few concessions to protesting students on 28 October — including a reform of Parcoursup and the creation of 15,000 additional seats in higher education — some parents started claiming that their children had been taken hostage by a minority of unyielding extremists. Some of these parents were also concerned about the challenge to authority — that of the state, as well as their own — posed by the student revolt. In Paris, Bordeaux, Marseille, Rennes or Montpellier, these infuriated parents organised on WhatsApp groups and started waking up at dawn to help the police contain the blockers. Forming human chains to protect students willing to go to class, they also tussled over the control of dustbins used by protesting students to block their lycées. In the ensuing scuffle, some students were hit and verbally abused by parents.

At Lycée Carnot, a prestigious public school in the 17th arrondissement of Paris, students told me that one of their schoolmates was the target of racist insults, while another received intimidating messages on his phone. For Adrien, a Senior Year student at Carnot, “These parents try to take the law into their own hands and, by doing so, they escalate violence because they make everyone furious.” School authorities are aware of this threat and the principal of another lycée in the 8th arrondissement, who asked to remain anonymous, said that he feared the opening of a “third front”, after those of students and cops, due to the counter-mobilisation of these parents.

Besides the risks of violent escalation, these initiatives seem to have mixed results. However menacing they try to be, parents are often outsmarted by the kids, who may give up blocking their school from outside only to foment trouble from within, leading school authorities to suspend activities anyway. As a result, hundreds of high schools (out of a total of 3,700) continue to be disturbed in the country — a figure which is difficult to verify since the Ministry of Education systematically scales down its statistics to convince public opinion that order has been restored. Whatever the exact figure, the return to normalcy remains elusive in many public schools and universities. While the kind of violence and looting witnessed on 17 October has not returned, tens of thousands of protesters continue to take to the streets every Saturday in major cities, with occasional skirmishes between them and the riot police.

Another Gen Z protest?

This ongoing student mobilisation shares characteristics with recent movements led by the Gen Z (composed of those born between 1997 and 2012) in Indonesia, Bangladesh, Nepal, Madagascar, Morocco or Peru. In France, even if labour unions started co-organising the protests from October 2026 onwards, the mobilisation has primarily involved youths between the ages of 15 and 25 years. This has infused it with a youthful energy and an irreverence characteristic of similar protests in the Global South and, more recently, across Europe (in Albania, Belgium, Italy and Germany). Especially in its early phase, the movement shared its horizontality with other youth revolts organised through Internet forums and communication apps such as LIHKG during the 2019 anti-ELAB movement in Hong Kong or Discord during more recent protests in Nepal and Morocco.

French students also draw on global cultural references that have provided young protesters worldwide with powerful role models. As Issa, a twenty-something protester who likes to dress up as Luffy, the main protagonist of One Piece, explained to me, “Luffy is the character who embodies freedom the best. He is devoted to living a free life. At the same time, he always cares for others. Whether in the manga or the anime, he always puts the interests of others ahead of his own, and those of the have nots ahead of those of the haves.” Coming from a Japanese manga and popularised by young Indonesians as a symbol of youthful rebellion, Luffy and his ragtag pirate crew are exemplary of the globalisation of popular culture and protest repertoires, which are no longer shaped exclusively by the West. Even the ubiquity of the three-finger salute drawn from the Hunger Games cannot be reduced to the success of Suzanne Collins’ books and their adaptation for the big screen. The gesture became a symbol of democracy and anti-authoritarian struggles in response to the Thai coup d’état of 2014, before being adopted by Hong Kong protesters the same year and by opponents to the military junta of Myanmar in 2021.

The analogy between the ongoing French student movement and other youthful protests of the past few years should not be overblown, however. In France, unlike in Nepal or Madagascar, the critique of elites has not been focusing on their nepotism but, rather, on their compromising with the capitalist class and the far right. A newly emerged theme, until then reserved to conspiracy theorists leaning to the far right, is that of ‘paedophile elites’ — a theme which seems to have been nurtured by the global scandal of the Epstein files but which has a special resonance among French youths due to the fact that President Emmanuel Macron was only 15 when he met his future wife Brigitte Trogneux, who at the time was 39 years old.

The deeply unpopular president has been a target of much criticism by young protesters. But even though some of them have been asking for his resignation, the movement has not put this demand at the forefront. Protesters do not really have the will — nor the means — to take down the government, the way their counterparts in Bangladesh, Nepal or Madagascar did. And while the government of Sébastien Lecornu was seriously rattled by the scenes of chaos of 17 October, it stood its ground and survived the storm. So far, it has only made minimal concessions to the protesters and does not seem ready to move further due to budgetary constraints. As a result, if some young activists strive to keep the movement afloat, most eyes are now set on the presidential election of April/May 2027, which could bring its own share of civil strife, possibly on an even grander scale.

item.title: Sheikh Hasina seeks to return to Bangladesh on December 16 on state carrier
item.description:
Ousted Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina plans to return home from more than two years of exile in India on December 16, her spokesperson told Reuters on Tuesday, though the government said she can only return through extradition.

It is the first time Hasina, 79, has set a specific date for her return, potentially raising political and legal tensions in a country where her party is banned and where violence has risen since she sought a new passport and other documents earlier this month.

In addition to seeking the paperwork, cancelled months after she fled to Delhi following the uprising against her, Hasina has urged the Bangladeshi government to arrange her return on flag carrier Biman Bangladesh Airlines.

“Since Sheikh Hasina was flown to India on a Bangladesh aircraft on August 5th, 2024, she now calls upon the government to arrange for her air transport from Delhi back to Dhaka,” the spokesperson, Syed Mozammel Ali, said in a statement.

“Having exiled her contrary to the Constitution under such circumstances, it is now the responsibility of the government to make possible her return to Bangladesh on Victory Day on December 16th.” The government, however, reiterated that she can only be extradited by India, having been sentenced to death by a Bangladeshi court last year in her absence for ordering a deadly crackdown on a student-led uprising. Hasina has denied the charges from exile.

“She can only return home by extradition treaty; in handcuffs, and under strict surveillance,” Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh’s minister of state for foreign affairs, told Reuters.

India’s foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In April, the ministry said it was examining Bangladesh’s extradition request and wanted to “engage constructively with the new government and further strengthen bilateral ties”.

On the request to arrange a flight, Kobir said: “Bangladesh will not entertain any such delusional request”.

Aminul Islam, chief prosecutor of Bangladesh’s International Crimes Tribunal, which sentenced Hasina to death, said it was unreasonable for a convicted fugitive to expect the government to arrange her return.

A Bangladeshi minister told Reuters on Sunday that Hasina would be arrested and jailed on return and that there had been no official discussions with India about sending an aircraft to bring her back.

The United Nations has said as many as 1,400 people were killed during the unrest that forced her out of power.

item.title: Seven health tests made mandatory for 2027 Hajj pilgrims before vaccination
item.description:
The government has made seven types of medical tests mandatory for pilgrims of the 2027 Hajj before they receive vaccinations.
The Religious Affairs Ministry issued a notice in this regard on Sunday.
According to the notice, pilgrims must undergo the tests at government hospitals at district and upazila levels or designated private hospitals across the country.
The mandatory tests include blood grouping and Rh typing, Complete Blood Count (CBC) with ESR, urine R/M/E, chest X-ray, electrocardiogram (ECG), random blood sugar (RBS) and serum creatinine.
Pilgrims suffering from chronic or serious illnesses may need additional medical examinations depending on their health conditions, it said.
For suspected heart failure, echocardiography will be required.
Pilgrims with kidney complications may need serum creatinine, ultrasonography of the kidneys and urinary bladder, and serum urea tests.
Those suspected of having liver complications will have to undergo serum bilirubin, SGPT, albumin-globulin ratio, whole-abdomen ultrasonography, upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy and prothrombin time tests.
For the detection of chronic lung diseases, sputum for acid-fast bacilli (AFB) testing and chest CT scans may be required, said the notice.
In cases involving pregnancy-related complications, a urine pregnancy test during the first three months and an ultrasonography under a pregnancy profile will be necessary.
Pilgrims must submit copies of their medical test reports and e-health profiles to the medical team at designated vaccination centres before receiving their vaccines.
A health certificate will be issued to pilgrims after they complete the vaccination process.
For information and assistance regarding Hajj, prospective pilgrims have been advised to contact the Hajj Call Centre at 16136.

item.title: Global dengue cases rise 34-fold in three decades
item.description:
Reported dengue cases worldwide have increased 34-fold over the past three decades, with South Asia among the regions experiencing the fastest growth, according to a new international study highlighting the disease's expanding geographical reach.
Presented at the annual meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene on Sunday in National Harbor, Maryland, the study estimates that 74 million dengue cases were reported across 143 countries between 1990 and 2024.
Of these, 10.7 million cases were missing from existing World Health Organization (WHO) databases, suggesting that global surveillance records have substantially underestimated reported infections.
The findings are particularly significant for Bangladesh, which is facing another major dengue outbreak.
According to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), 173,473 patients have been hospitalized and 518 have died from dengue between January 1 and Sunday this year.
In the 24 hours until 8am on Sunday, two more people died and 1,519 patients were admitted to hospitals nationwide. Dhaka Division recorded the highest number of new admissions, at 755.
Speaking to Dhaka Tribune, Dr Ahyoung Lim, the study's lead researcher from the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine (LSHTM), said South Asia was among the regions experiencing the fastest growth in reported dengue incidence.
The increase was particularly rapid in regions where dengue has emerged more recently, including Africa, the Middle East and South Asia, compared with some regions where the disease has been endemic for longer.
However, the study does not explain the sharp rise in reported cases.
Lim said climate, urbanisation and international travel are commonly considered important factors in dengue transmission, but the research did not examine their individual contributions.
“The faster growth in Africa, the Middle East and South Asia is likely to be due to both real spread and to improved recognition and diagnosis in countries which only very recently have been reporting dengue,” he said.
This distinction matters because rising reported cases may reflect both an actual expansion of dengue transmission and better detection and surveillance.
Bangladesh has experienced increasingly severe dengue outbreaks in recent years, with 2023 marking the worst on record.
DGHS recorded 321,179 hospitalizations and 1,705 deaths in 2023, followed by 101,214 hospitalizations and 575 deaths in 2024, and 102,861 hospitalisations and 413 deaths in 2025.
The 2026 outbreak has already surpassed the number of hospitalizations recorded in either of the previous two years, with more than 173,000 patients admitted by November 22.
The new study offers a broader picture of dengue trends by reconstructing historical estimates for periods and locations where surveillance data were incomplete.
Lim said the research team had made its country-level estimates publicly available, including monthly and annual figures with corresponding uncertainty intervals.
The dataset includes Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, Nepal and Sri Lanka, allowing researchers to examine historical trends in reported dengue cases across South Asia.
However, the researchers did not rank individual countries by incidence or growth, noting that differences in surveillance and reporting could affect comparisons.
“Our paper is about global and regional trends and doesn't involve any country rankings,” Lim said.
He added that variations between countries could reflect differences in surveillance and reporting rather than actual differences in dengue transmission.
Dengue is primarily transmitted by infected Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, which thrive in urban areas where stagnant water provides breeding sites.
Temperature, rainfall and humidity influence mosquito survival, breeding patterns and the potential for virus transmission. Rapid urbanisation, population movement and international travel can also contribute to the geographical spread of dengue.
Lim said these factors were relevant to emerging hotspots such as Bangladesh, although the study did not assess their individual contributions.
“Temperature, rainfall and urbanisation are all known to impact the mosquitoes that carry dengue and are often regarded as key factors in the emergence of hotspots such as Bangladesh,” he said.
He added that the study's estimates could provide a foundation for further research into the environmental and human factors shaping dengue transmission.
The research also highlights the importance of strengthening disease surveillance, particularly in countries where limited diagnostic capacity and inconsistent reporting may obscure the actual scale of outbreaks.
