item.title: Democrats win largest US House majority since 1992
item.description:
Democrats have won the largest majority in the US House of Representatives in more than three decades, after Chuck Hubbard defeated Republican representative Virginia Foxx in North Carolina, US media projected on Sunday.
The party won full control of both the House and Senate in a sweeping midterm rout with a landslide of upsets that delivered a crushing rebuke of President Donald Trump and his Republican Party.
CBS News and NBC News projected Hubbard’s win on Sunday, securing the Democrats a 258th seat in Congress’ 435-member House.
The majority is the largest won by either party since 1992, when Bill Clinton won the presidency and Democrats won a total of 258 seats.
It also beats the 257 seats won when Barack Obama was elected president in 2008 but falls short of the 334-seat majority the party won at the end of the 1930s, which is the largest on record.
Republicans have not controlled more than 250 House seats since the start of the Great Depression which saw mass unemployment, acute deflation and widespread poverty.
“House Democrats have just secured the largest majority any party in Congress has held this century. BOOM,” House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said in a post on X.
The 56-year-old New Yorker is poised to become the first Black speaker of the House, after being nominated by his party.
Sunday’s result came after Foxx requested a recount.
Hubbard said Sunday that he had spoken with Foxx, who “graciously conceded following the results of the recount process.”
“Let me be the first to thank Congresswoman Foxx for her decades of service and countless sacrifices,” he added on X.
Roy Cooper, the state’s former governor, won election to the Senate, becoming the first Democrat elected to the Senate from North Carolina since 2008.
Four other House races remain outstanding: one each in Minnesota and Tennessee and two in Louisiana that are heading to a December runoff.
The Democrats midterm triumph hands the party the power to block Trump’s agenda and investigate alleged corruption for the last two years of his presidency.
Democrats have already unveiled plans for wide-ranging investigations into Trump officials and his business interests when they take control of the lower chamber in January.
Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, sent 12 letters on Wednesday, warning members of Trump’s family and senior administration figures to preserve documents ahead of investigations into alleged corruption, immigration abuses and the handling of files related to sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
The administration has pushed back against the threatened scrutiny.
November’s midterm results reflected deep anger over living costs, tariffs and Trump’s war against Iran, which has sent fuel prices soaring and compounded dissatisfaction with an already deeply unpopular president.

item.title: Iran says will use ‘all available means’ to counter US blockade
item.description:
Iran said Monday it would use all means at its disposal to counter a US naval blockade that was imposed in retaliation for its own push to block the Strait of Hormuz.
“We will certainly not tolerate these actions and will use all available means to counter US aggression,” said foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei in a weekly press briefing.
War broke out between Iran and the United States on February 28 when US-Israeli strikes killed the Islamic republic’s supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
The conflict has since expanded after Iran retaliated with missile and drone strikes across the region and with militant groups it backs in Lebanon, Yemen and Iraq also entering the fray.
The Strait of Hormuz has become the focus of the conflict, with Iran continuing in its efforts to blockade the waterway, vital to global energy supplies.
In response, the US imposed its own counterblockade of Iranian ports. It later announced a raft of economic sanctions, and launched a task force to disrupt land routes into Iran.
“You should bear in mind that what the Americans have described as economic sanctions, an economic blockade and a naval blockade undoubtedly constitutes an act of military aggression against Iran,” said Baqaei.
“Under these circumstances, Iran is entitled, pursuant to Article 51 of the UN Charter, to use any means at its disposal to defend itself.”
Iranian forces have made multiple announcements in recent weeks of ships catching fire attempting to use routes that Tehran considers off-limits.
Diplomatic efforts to resolve the crisis remain stalled, especially since the collapse of a June deal that laid out a pathway to a permanent settlement.
Iran has said Hormuz could be open within two days but only if Washington agreed to its list of demands which include the lifting of the blockade.
“If the American side fulfils its commitments, security can be restored to the Strait of Hormuz and the region in the shortest possible time,” said Baqaei.

item.title: July Charter back in focus as government and opposition remain divided
item.description:
Although the ruling party has spoken of political unity against sabotage, the July National Charter is once again being raised repeatedly by the parliamentary opposition. Questions have arisen about how it will be implemented and where the obstacles lie in reaching a final outcome. Will the government and the opposition ultimately reach any agreement?
Discussions on the charter are gaining renewed momentum after the prime minister began a dialogue with leaders of the National Citizen Party (NCP) on Monday (November 23), amid the country's ongoing situation. Similar meetings with other parties are expected to be held in phases.
After the meeting, the NCP said it would not form political unity solely to prevent the Awami League or around December.
Returning from London on Sunday (November 22), NCP convener and opposition chief whip Nahid Islam told reporters at the airport that the July Charter must be implemented in accordance with the people's verdict in the referendum. He said the trial of the genocide must be expedited. He also called for the Constitution Amendment Committee to be cancelled, describing it as a one-party committee.
At a rally in the capital on Saturday (November 21), Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami Secretary General Mia Golam Porwar, whose party is the main opposition, said they would remain active against Awami League sabotage. However, he said they would consider the issue of unity only if the government implemented the referendum verdict and the July Charter.
Prime Minister's Adviser Mahdi Amin said on Monday that the NCP had actually made no demands during its meeting with the head of government.
He said the BNP government would implement the July Charter in full while accepting the "Note of Dissent". The adviser to the Prime Minister's Office added that the government would fully implement its election manifesto, which it had presented in the same manner as the Note of Dissent.
Some have expressed doubts about whether the charter will ultimately see the light of day, given the uncompromising positions of both sides.
The government and the opposition disagree on several issues regarding constitutional amendments. The main dispute, however, concerns the implementation of the referendum verdict under the July National Charter Implementation Order.
The July National Charter, adopted on April 17, 2025, contains 84 reform proposals. Of these, 48 are directly related to constitutional amendments, while the remaining 36 can be implemented through the enactment or amendment of laws.
According to the opposition, they do not want to go beyond the president's reform order, but the government is violating it.
During the interim government's tenure, the "July National Charter (Constitutional Reform) Implementation Order" was issued on November 13, 2025. It stated that a Constitution Reform Council would be convened within 30 days and its work completed within 180 days.
In the referendum, four questions were combined into a single Yes or No vote, and Yes won.
BNP members of parliament took their oath as MPs in accordance with the party's decision, but did not take the additional oath as members of the Constitution Reform Council. Instead, they formed a Constitution Amendment Committee. As a result, the Constitution Reform Council was never formed.
Members of parliament from Jamaat-e-Islami and the NCP took both oaths, and they remain firm in their support for constitutional reform. Several leaders from both sides have said this is essentially why implementation of the July Charter is being obstructed.
The ruling BNP wants constitutional amendments. Accordingly, a 17-member committee was initially formed, including five opposition members of parliament. The opposition rejected it.
On November 11, the committee was reconstituted as the 12-member "Constitution Amendment Committee", removing the opposition members' names. Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed was made its chairman.
The NCP has also demanded the committee's cancellation. After Monday afternoon's meeting with the prime minister, Nahid Islam said they had recommended cancelling it. He called for giving importance to reform, justice and the country's sovereignty before establishing national unity.
NCP joint convener Monira Sharmin told Dhaka Tribune on Monday night: "According to the July Charter and the referendum verdict, a Constitution Reform Committee was supposed to be formed. But the government has disobeyed this and unilaterally formed a “Constitution Amendment Committee” according to its own wishes. Therefore, we have demanded the cancellation of the government's decision."
She said the party had demanded constitutional reform by cancelling the committee. The NCP also demanded the execution of the death sentences of Sheikh Hasina and other accused in the July genocide cases, as well as the rehabilitation of the families of martyrs and the injured.
"Although the government speaks of unity, it is not accepting any suggestions from the opposition," Monira Sharmin said. "We raised these issues with the prime minister."
Jamaat-e-Islami Central Executive Council member and Dhaka-12 MP Md Saiful Alam also spoke to Dhaka Tribune.
"The government has deceived the people by denying the referendum verdict," he said. "This is because there has never been a precedent in the past of forming a special committee during constitutional amendments. We do not understand why it happened this time."
He said several previous amendments had been cancelled by the courts. For this reason, he said, the opposition did not join the Constitution Amendment Committee.
Discussions with several government and opposition sources have revealed that implementation of the July Charter is essentially stuck within the confines of reform versus amendment.
The uncompromising positions of the two sides have created uncertainty. Questions are also being raised about whether the problem will be resolved, or whether the process will become visible at all.
Bangladesh Socialist Party (BASAD) General Secretary Bazlur Rashid Firoz said: "The original Constitution of 1972 was comparatively democratic. However, it also had some limitations and weaknesses. We have said from the beginning that, with changes over time, these weaknesses need to be removed to make the Constitution more democratic."
He said the Constitution has undergone 17 amendments, but necessary amendments have not been made in the interests of the people and to establish a democratic system.
He said his party had spoken about amending Article 70, constitutional recognition of various ethnic communities including indigenous people, and equal rights for men and women in property inheritance. They had also demanded the independence, neutrality and separate secretariats of the Election Commission, the Public Service Commission (PSC), the Anti-Corruption Commission and the judiciary.
"These reforms are essential to establish democracy and the rule of law," he said. "But the government has not implemented even one of these proposals."
He added: "It is necessary to reach agreement on issues where minimum consensus is possible for establishing democracy. However, instead of reaching that minimum consensus, several parties, including the BNP, Jamaat and NCP, have tried to impose their own positions on others. As a result, the July Charter was not adopted unanimously, and different parties have Notes of Dissent. We did not sign the charter because we have differences of opinion over several of its recommendations and proposals to change the fundamental principles of the Constitution."
BNP Standing Committee member Selima Rahman expressed a different view. She told Dhaka Tribune: "The government is not against the referendum verdict or the July Charter. However, the BNP is in favour of resolving the matter in accordance with the Constitution. In this light, the opposition was also included in the Constitution Amendment Committee. But they did not respond to our call. We think it is important for them to understand the matter deeply in this regard."

item.title: Yunus: Attacks on Grameen Bank are attacks on poor women
item.description:
Nearly 100 branches of Grameen Bank across Bangladesh have come under petrol bomb attacks since the beginning of November, former chief adviser Professor Muhammad Yunus alleged on Monday, warning that the continuing violence threatens the safety and livelihoods of millions of poor women.
In a statement issued on November 23, Yunus said attacks on the bank’s branches had become an almost daily occurrence, with employees and borrowers narrowly escaping potentially deadly incidents.
He alleged that attackers had chanted the slogan “Joy Bangla” during the incidents and that the repeated pattern suggested the attacks were being carried out under instructions from higher authorities.
Yunus called for immediate and effective measures to stop the violence and demanded that those responsible be brought to justice without delay.
Describing the attacks as a direct assault on the security and economic independence of poor women, Yunus said Grameen Bank served as a lifeline for millions of rural families.
He said 97% of the bank’s 11 million borrowers were women and that its loan recovery rate exceeded 95%.
According to Yunus, the bank’s borrowers depend on its services to support their families, finance their children’s education and meet everyday expenses.
He warned that the continuing attacks were creating fear among rural women who relied on the institution for financial security.
The former chief adviser also emphasised that he had no ownership stake or management role in Grameen Bank.
He said 90% of the bank’s shares belonged to its borrowers, while the government held the remaining 10%.
Yunus recalled that the Awami League government removed him as the bank’s managing director in 2011.
Since then, he said, he had played no role in its management or operations.
He also stressed that he had never personally owned shares in Grameen Bank.
Yunus said the violence extended beyond Grameen Bank branches.
He cited the reported arson attack on the home of July uprising leader Nusrat Tabassum, as well as attacks on the residences of three BNP lawmakers and three police stations.
He described the incidents as part of a wider pattern of violence that required urgent intervention.
According to the statement, Grameen Bank has requested additional security from the Ministry of Home Affairs to protect its borrowers, employees and important documents.
The bank has also sought measures to ensure that its services to low-income women continue without disruption.
Yunus thanked law enforcement agencies for steps already taken in response to the attacks but called for stronger action to prevent further incidents.
He urged authorities to identify and prosecute those involved in planning and carrying out the attacks.
The former chief adviser also appealed to supporters of Grameen Bank around the world to speak out against the violence and stand beside the institution and its borrowers.

item.title: Bangladesh outlines education initiatives to UN rapporteur
item.description:
Secretary (Bilateral) at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs Dr Md Nazrul Islam on Tuesday outlined the government's key education initiatives during a meeting with United Nations (UN) Special Rapporteur on the Right to Education Farida Shaheed in Dhaka.
During the meeting, Nazrul Islam highlighted initiatives to extend free education for girls up to graduate level and strengthen technical, vocational and technology-based education.
He also briefed Shaheed on government plans to expand educational opportunities for children in remote and underserved areas.
Welcoming Shaheed to Bangladesh, Nazrul Islam reaffirmed the government's commitment to ensuring inclusive, equitable and quality education for all.
He expressed hope that the visit would facilitate constructive dialogue and meaningful engagement on various aspects of the right to education. He also hoped that the observations and recommendations emerging from the visit would contribute to the government's ongoing efforts to strengthen the education sector.
Nazrul Islam assured Shaheed of the government's full cooperation throughout her visit.
In response, Shaheed thanked the government for the warm welcome and facilitation of her visit.
She said she looked forward to learning about Bangladesh's education policies, initiatives and challenges through discussions with government officials, civil society groups and others working in the sector.
Shaheed is visiting Bangladesh from November 23 to December 4. This is her first visit to the country in her capacity as the UN Special Rapporteur on the Right to Education.
During her stay, she is scheduled to meet representatives of relevant government ministries, divisions and agencies, visit educational institutions, and engage with civil society organizations and other relevant stakeholders.

item.title: Zelensky calls for four-way talks with Russia ‘as soon as possible’
item.description:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Monday called for new negotiations with Russia involving European leaders to be held as soon as possible and repeated a plea for his country to join the Nato alliance.
Zelensky, speaking by video to a gathering of lawmakers from Nato countries in Berlin, welcomed the latest push for peace talks with Moscow.
“We must do everything to make sure that the four-party meeting -- Ukraine, Europe, America and Russia -- happens as soon as possible. We are ready to do this. Literally tomorrow,” Zelensky said.
“We have heard from our partners that they want to try to make it happen before Christmas. We hope it happens sooner.”
European governments have been excluded from past discussions and their push to join talks has gained prominence in recent weeks.
Zelensky, whose country has been battling a full-scale Russian invasion since February 2022, has repeatedly called for a path to full membership in Nato -- and not simply receiving security guarantees from alliance countries.
He argued that Ukraine’s combat experience, innovative defense industry and large military would all benefit other allies.
“Nato is the answer -- and with a strong Ukrainian army, Nato itself is guaranteed to be stronger,” Zelensky told the Berlin gathering.
A number of Nato leaders have expressed hesitation about bringing Ukraine into the alliance.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte, speaking after Zelensky at the same event on Monday, underscored the alliance’s support for Ukraine but noted that joining would require unanimous support.
“Not all Nato allies agree at this moment (on) letting Ukraine become a member,” Rutte said, though he also firmly rejected the idea that outside powers like Russia could dictate who joins the alliance.
During a gathering of Ukrainian supporters in Berlin last week, US envoy Jared Kushner said that Washington might consider offering Ukraine a security guarantee similar to that provided under Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty as part of a peace settlement.
But in his remarks on Monday, Zelensky said major questions remain about how such guarantees would work without a full Nato commitment.
“Which countries will support Ukraine if Ukraine is attacked again? What exactly will our partners do in response? Which troops will be stationed on our territory in advance? How much will all this cost? And will it really work?
“All of this is not easy and so far we have not heard clear specific answers,” Zelensky said.
The Ukrainian leader also repeated a call for Nato countries to provide more air defense weapons, urging them to empty their stockpiles to allow Ukraine to repel Russian airstrikes.
“Missiles that can stop Russian ballistic missiles should not be sitting in warehouses collecting dust,” he said.
